scope: All effective Contracts, Civil Procedure and other non-LRS connection explanation groups in the saved pre-correction snapshot.
method: Read all 1,742 distinct strings with every endpoint pair and edge ID. Compare legal scope with the already completed 391 canonical Holding/rule introduction review, targeted complete saved Reasoning rereads, prior rule/source reviews, and selected fresh primary passages. Membership and source-reference links were screened as structural prose; this does not freshly verify every assignment against its syllabus. No-change screening is not a universal legal-accuracy certification.

input.effectiveBasis: Saved default authored effective graph after assembler overlays; user-saved edits are not represented. The snapshot intentionally predates root integration of these and LRS proposals.

readingBatchNote: Overlapping bounded reads filled truncated output. The final coverage includes each entire explanation and every endpoint pair. Most membership links use repeated assignment prose; endpoints and edge IDs were retained.

Subject-matter jurisdiction is a court’s authority to decide a category of dispute. Federal courts require an applicable grant of authority within the limits allowed by the Constitution.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Personal jurisdiction is a court’s authority to bind a particular person or entity through its judgment. It concerns the defendant’s relationship to the forum or a separate recognized basis for submitting to that authority.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: A court may need both a statute authorizing its action and constitutional permission to exercise that authority. The Constitution can allow a reach that the legislature has chosen not to grant.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: A procedural ruling decides how or whether litigation may proceed. A merits determination decides the parties’ underlying legal entitlement, although some motions can resolve that entitlement without trial.

source.title: Procedural rulings and decisions on the merits

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Waiver or forfeiture can prevent a party from relying on an objection that was available earlier. The consequences depend on the kind of objection and the governing rule.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: A precedent’s contribution depends on what the court decided, the facts and posture before it, and which reasoning commanded the necessary votes. A dissent or concurrence can illuminate a dispute without becoming the holding of the Court.

source.title: Holding, separate opinion, and doctrinal development

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Federalism distributes judicial and lawmaking responsibilities between the national government and the states. Procedure can affect that distribution through jurisdiction, governing law, and the treatment of state-created rights.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Procedural design affects whether parties can obtain a meaningful decision and what obtaining one costs. The course repeatedly examines the tradeoff between access to proof and protection against costly, weakly supported litigation.

source.title: Access, cost, and the opportunity for a merits decision

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Judicial discretion is the authority a rule or doctrine gives a judge to choose among legally permissible responses after considering relevant facts and interests. The authority remains bounded by the governing law.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: The territorial approach associated with Pennoyer linked a state court’s authority to service, consent, domicile-related settings, and property within its territory. It provides the historical starting point for the course’s personal-jurisdiction sequence.

Domicile connects a person to a state through residence and the legally relevant intention to make it a home. In the readings it matters both to citizenship for diversity and to certain bases of judicial authority.

Minimum contacts describe the forum connections needed to make an assertion of personal jurisdiction compatible with the due-process standard developed in International Shoe. The inquiry examines the quality, nature, and legal significance of the connections.

Purposeful availment concerns conduct by which a defendant deliberately engages with a forum and invokes the benefits or protections associated with that activity. Some contexts describe purposeful direction of conduct toward the forum.

Specific jurisdiction requires an appropriate connection between the defendant’s forum activity and the particular litigation. The assigned cases describe claims that arise out of or relate to those contacts.

source.title: The connection between forum activity and the claim

reviewedGroups.text: The fairness inquiry evaluates whether exercising jurisdiction is reasonable in light of the burdens and interests identified in the personal-jurisdiction cases. It operates within the governing jurisdictional framework.
Specific jurisdiction is authority to decide a claim connected to the defendant’s forum contacts. It is claim-linked, so the relationship among defendant, forum, and litigation must be identified.

General jurisdiction permits a court to hear claims against a defendant without requiring those claims to arise from forum activity. For a corporation, the assigned cases focus on whether it is essentially at home in the forum.

source.title: General jurisdiction and being at home

reviewedGroups.text: The stream-of-commerce problem asks when a manufacturer’s distribution of a product through others supplies a sufficient connection to the state where litigation is brought. It is especially difficult when the manufacturer does not directly sell to the ultimate forum customer.

The effects cases examine when intentional conduct directed toward a forum supplies a jurisdictional connection even though the actor worked elsewhere. The defendant’s connection to the forum remains essential.

A contract can create forum connections through the parties’ deliberate relationship, negotiations, future obligations, and performance. The existence of a contract with a forum resident is only part of the inquiry.
A long-arm statute authorizes jurisdiction over persons outside the state in defined circumstances. Its interpretation determines the state-law reach before constitutional limits are applied.

Consent supplies a basis for personal jurisdiction through an agreement, conduct in litigation, or another legally recognized submission to the court’s authority. The assigned cases examine both how consent arises and its limits.
An agreement identifies where the parties will litigate covered disputes.

Jurisdictional discovery develops evidence concerning facts needed to decide the court’s authority over a party. A defendant’s objection to jurisdiction does not necessarily remove the court’s power to require information needed to decide that objection.

Tag jurisdiction refers to personal jurisdiction based on serving an individual while the individual is physically present in the state. Burnham upheld its use on the facts before the Court, with differing reasons.

source.title: Personal service while in the forum

reviewedGroups.text: Property-based jurisdiction uses a defendant’s interests in property as part of the basis for adjudication. The course distinguishes disputes about the property itself from efforts to use unrelated property to obtain leverage over a person.

Internet-jurisdiction questions ask which online activities connect a particular defendant to a particular forum. The ability to access a site everywhere creates a need to identify meaningful forum-directed conduct.

A collateral challenge contests a judgment’s authority in a later proceeding rather than through ordinary review in the original action. Personal-jurisdiction choices can affect whether such a challenge remains open.

target.title: Finality and the binding effect of judgments

reviewedGroups.text: Finality limits repeated litigation after a court has entered a judgment. The course encounters it in jurisdictional challenges, class representation, and the protection of absent persons.

source.title: Finality and the binding effect of judgments

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Notice is the communication needed to give an affected person a meaningful opportunity to protect an interest before a court acts. Mullane evaluates whether the method is reasonably calculated, under the circumstances, to inform interested persons.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Service of process is the formal delivery or legally authorized communication of the summons and complaint or equivalent initiating papers. It tells a defendant that a judicial proceeding requires a response.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: A court may refuse to recognize service when deception procured a defendant’s presence for that purpose. The separate doctrine of immunity can protect persons present for judicial proceedings in specified circumstances.

source.title: Presence procured by fraud and service immunity

reviewedGroups.text: Due process protects persons affected by governmental adjudication through requirements of appropriate authority, notice, and an opportunity to be heard. The required protection depends on the setting and the interests at risk.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: An opportunity to be heard allows an affected person to challenge the grounds for governmental action before an appropriate decision-maker. Timing and the form of the hearing depend on the legal setting.

A prejudgment remedy restricts possession or use of property before final determination of liability. Attachment, garnishment, and replevin can protect a claimant but can also harm a person before the claim is proven.

The Mathews framework evaluates the private interest, the risk of error and value of additional safeguards, and the relevant governmental or countervailing interests. Doehr applies an adapted inquiry to a private litigant’s use of attachment.

source.title: Balancing the safeguards required by due process

reviewedGroups.text: Diversity jurisdiction permits specified civil actions between parties of different citizenship to be heard in federal court when the statutory conditions are met. The ordinary statute combines citizenship requirements with an amount in controversy.
Citizenship identifies the legally relevant state or foreign affiliation of a party for diversity jurisdiction. It depends on the kind of party rather than a single universal test.

The amount in controversy is the value genuinely placed in dispute for a jurisdictional statute. It is assessed by the governing legal standard and the claim at issue, rather than simply the amount eventually awarded.

Aggregation concerns when several claims may be added together to satisfy a jurisdictional amount. The answer depends on the parties and whether the claims are separate or share a common undivided interest.

Standing asks whether the party invoking federal judicial power has the constitutionally required personal stake in the requested relief. The assigned discussion emphasizes concrete injury and its relationship to the challenged conduct and remedy.

Federal-question jurisdiction concerns actions arising under federal law within the applicable jurisdictional grant. Federal creation of the cause of action supplies the principal route, while a narrow category of state-law claims can also qualify.

The well-pleaded complaint rule looks to the plaintiff’s own claim for federal-question jurisdiction. A federal defense anticipated in the complaint ordinarily does not make a state-law claim arise under federal law.

A narrow category of state-law claims can arise under federal law when resolving the claim necessarily requires deciding an actually disputed and substantial federal issue in a manner consistent with the federal-state division of judicial responsibility.

Supplemental jurisdiction allows a federal court with an authorized anchor claim to hear certain related claims that lack an independent federal jurisdictional basis. The statute imposes conditions, exclusions, and grounds for declining the additional claims.

Pendent and ancillary jurisdiction are historical descriptions of federal authority over related claims or parties. Congress’s enactment of § 1367 provides the statutory framework emphasized in the later course materials.

source.title: From pendent and ancillary jurisdiction to § 1367

reviewedGroups.text: The pendent-party problem asks whether a related claim against or by an additional person may be heard when that person’s claim has no independent federal jurisdictional basis.
When original jurisdiction rests solely on diversity, § 1367(b) restricts certain additional claims by plaintiffs and proposed plaintiffs. The role of each party and the method of joinder matter.

Even when supplemental judicial power exists, the court may have grounds to decline to exercise it. The assigned materials connect that choice to state-law complexity, predominance, loss of federal claims, and other exceptional circumstances.

source.title: When a court may decline related state claims

reviewedGroups.text: Removal transfers an eligible action from state court to federal court through a procedure authorized by Congress. It ordinarily depends on federal original jurisdiction and the removing party’s statutory role.

source.title: Removal from state to federal court

target.title: Removal from state to federal court

reviewedGroups.text: The forum-defendant rule restricts specified diversity removals when a properly joined and served defendant is a citizen of the forum state. It is a statutory restriction beyond the existence of diversity jurisdiction.

target.title: Removal from state to federal court

reviewedGroups.text: Venue identifies the geographically proper court within the relevant court system. It allocates the location of litigation and is distinct from subject-matter jurisdiction and personal jurisdiction.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: The historical local-action rule associated certain claims involving land with courts where the land was located. The readings examine the rule’s origins, contested rationale, and later statutory treatment.

source.title: Local actions and territorial land disputes

reviewedGroups.text: Transfer moves litigation from one federal district to another under statutory authority. Different statutes address a convenient alternative to a proper venue, an improper venue, and coordinated pretrial proceedings.

source.title: 28 U.S.C. § 1404 — transfer from a proper venue

reviewedGroups.text: Forum non conveniens permits dismissal in favor of an available adequate alternative forum when the governing balance strongly favors litigation there. It often matters when transfer within the federal system cannot reach the alternative forum.

Erie addresses the law a federal court uses when adjudicating rights governed by state law. Federal jurisdiction alone does not authorize creation of a federal general common law to replace state rules of decision.

source.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed
Governing law in federal court: Erie

reviewedGroups.text: Before Erie, Swift permitted federal courts to exercise independent judgment on some questions categorized as general law. Erie rejected that approach to state-law rights and required respect for state judicial decisions as well as statutes.

source.title: Swift, Erie, and federal general common law

target.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie

reviewedGroups.text: The outcome inquiry asks how a difference between state and federal treatment affects the enforcement of state-created rights. Hanna relates the inquiry to discouraging forum shopping and unequal administration of law.

source.title: Outcome effects and Erie’s twin aims

target.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie

reviewedGroups.text: Byrd examines whether a federal court should follow a state practice assigning a disputed factual issue to a judge rather than a jury. The analysis considers the state rule’s connection to substantive rights and the federal system’s interests.

source.title: State interests and the federal judge–jury allocation

target.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie

reviewedGroups.text: A scope inquiry asks whether the federal provision actually answers the disputed procedural question. A direct conflict requires a different analysis from a situation in which the state and federal provisions can operate together.

source.title: Does a federal statute or Federal Rule govern?

target.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie

reviewedGroups.text: The Rules Enabling Act authorizes general federal rules of practice and procedure while limiting their effect on substantive rights. It supplies a validity inquiry for Federal Rules distinct from the ordinary Erie choice when no such Rule governs.

target.title: Does a federal statute or Federal Rule govern?

reviewedGroups.text: Accommodation asks whether the relevant state and federal interests can both be respected through a particular allocation of tasks or procedure. Gasperini considers review of damages under state law and federal appellate constraints.

target.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie

reviewedGroups.text: Choice of law identifies which jurisdiction’s substantive law governs a claim. This is separate from whether a court has authority over the case and parties.

target.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie

reviewedGroups.text: Specialized federal common law consists of judicially developed federal rules supported by particular federal interests or authority, rather than a general power arising from federal jurisdiction.

target.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie

reviewedGroups.text: Boyle recognizes a defined defense to certain state design-defect claims when imposing liability would significantly conflict with federal procurement decisions. It is a specialized federal common-law doctrine.

source.title: The federal contractor defense in Boyle

reviewedGroups.text: The reverse-Erie problem concerns the obligations of a state court adjudicating a federal claim. State procedure cannot be used in a way that impermissibly defeats the federal right and its protected incidents.

source.title: Federal rights enforced in state court

target.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie

reviewedGroups.text: A release purports to surrender a legal claim. When the claim arises under a federal statute, federal law may govern whether a challenged release validly extinguishes that right.

target.title: Federal rights enforced in state court

reviewedGroups.text: A pleading states a party’s claims or responses in the form required by the applicable procedural rules. A complaint must provide a sufficient account of entitlement to relief to move the case forward.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Notice pleading emphasizes giving the opposing party an intelligible account of the claim and its grounds without requiring the technical formulas of older pleading systems. The assigned cases trace its development and later qualifications.

Plausibility asks whether the well-pleaded factual allegations support a reasonable inference of entitlement to relief in the context of the claim. Legal labels and recitations of elements do not supply missing facts.

A claim passes through different tests as litigation proceeds. Pleading concerns sufficient allegations; the production burden concerns enough evidence for a reasonable verdict; persuasion concerns whether the factfinder is convinced under the governing standard.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Rule 9(b) requires particular circumstances for allegations of fraud or mistake. The requirement concerns the pleaded theory, not simply the title of the statute under which the party sues.

The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act imposes a heightened pleading requirement concerning scienter, the legally required wrongful state of mind, in the securities setting addressed by Tellabs.

Special-damage pleading identifies losses that require particular notice rather than being sufficiently conveyed by the ordinary consequences of the pleaded wrong. The classification depends on the governing law and the claim.

Rule 12 provides distinct ways to respond to a complaint, including objections to authority, legal sufficiency, excessive vagueness, and specified material within the pleading. Each motion has its own purpose and preservation rules.

A privilege can protect conduct or statements that might otherwise support liability. The assigned Garcia opinion distinguishes conditional protection, which may depend on facts such as malice, from absolute protection for particular proceedings.

source.title: Privilege as a response to a pleaded claim

reviewedGroups.text: An answer responds to the complaint’s allegations by admitting them, denying them, or properly stating insufficient knowledge. Those responses define what remains disputed.

source.title: Admissions, denials, and lack of knowledge

reviewedGroups.text: An affirmative defense supplies an additional reason the defendant should avoid or limit liability even when the claim’s ordinary allegations are assumed. It performs a different role from a denial.

Amendment changes a party’s pleading as the case develops. The rules distinguish changes allowed without permission from those requiring consent or leave of court, and address the effect on timing and trial.

source.title: Federal Rule 15 — amendment and relation back

reviewedGroups.text: Relation back treats a qualifying amendment as connected to the original pleading for limitations purposes. Different provisions govern changed allegations and changed defendants.

source.title: Relation back of an amended claim or party

reviewedGroups.text: An issue not stated in the pleadings may become part of the case when the parties expressly or impliedly consent to trying it. The evidence and conduct of the parties must support that conclusion.

Certification and verification requirements attach responsibility to statements submitted to the court. Sanctions can enforce that responsibility but require the applicable substantive standard and procedural protections.

The safe-harbor mechanism gives a party an opportunity to withdraw or correct challenged material before an opponent’s Rule 11 motion is filed with the court. It is a procedural condition on that route to sanctions.

Joinder determines which claims and persons can be included in one action. Different devices govern multiple claims, counterclaims, crossclaims, additional defendants, required parties, interpleader, and intervention.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: The real party in interest is the person entitled under the governing substantive law to enforce the right asserted. The inquiry can change when rights are assigned or an insurer becomes subrogated to a claim.
Claim joinder allows a party to assert more than one claim against an existing opposing party. Federal Rule 18 provides broad procedural permission even when claims differ in subject or legal theory.

source.title: Multiple claims against an opposing party

target.title: Multiple claims against an opposing party

reviewedGroups.text: A counterclaim is a claim against an opposing party. Rule 13 distinguishes compulsory claims arising from the relevant transaction or occurrence from permissive claims that may be asserted without that connection.
Transaction and occurrence connect events for particular joinder rules. The inquiry often considers their logical and factual relationship rather than requiring identical legal theories or documents.

A crossclaim is a claim against a coparty, such as one defendant’s claim against another defendant. Rule 13(g) requires the specified connection to the transaction, occurrence, or property involved in the action.

Rule 20 permits multiple plaintiffs or defendants when the claims have the required transaction-or-series connection and share a question of law or fact. It allows related individual claims to proceed in one action.

Rule 19 asks whether an absent person should be joined and, if joinder is not feasible, whether the action can fairly proceed without that person. The inquiry protects existing parties, absentees, and the interest in complete resolution.

A judgment ordinarily does not bind a person who was neither a party nor represented through a recognized exception. Yet litigation can still practically impair an absentee’s interests even without formally binding that person.
Impleader brings a nonparty into an action because that person may owe the defending party all or part of the liability asserted by the plaintiff. Common examples involve indemnity or contribution.

Interpleader allows a stakeholder facing competing demands for the same property or obligation to bring the claimants into one proceeding. It protects against inconsistent obligations while providing a process to decide entitlement.

source.title: Interpleader: competing demands on one obligation

target.title: Interpleader: competing demands on one obligation

reviewedGroups.text: Statutory interpleader is a specific federal jurisdictional route for competing claims to money or property. The readings distinguish its minimal-diversity, fund, service, venue, and injunction provisions from ordinary Rule 22 interpleader.

target.title: Interpleader: competing demands on one obligation

reviewedGroups.text: Sovereign immunity can prevent a state or foreign sovereign from being joined in litigation without an applicable exception or waiver. When that sovereign claims an interest in the dispute, its absence also affects the Rule 19 analysis.

Intervention is a procedure by which a person outside the lawsuit seeks to enter it to protect an interest or participate under the rule’s conditions. Rule 24 distinguishes intervention of right from permissive intervention.

A court can coordinate related litigation or separate issues for trial without treating every procedural unit as one merged claim. These management choices seek efficiency while limiting prejudice and confusion.

source.title: Federal Rule 42 — consolidation and separate trials

reviewedGroups.text: Joinder combines claims of persons who are individually parties. A class action allows named representatives to litigate for absentees after satisfying the requirements for legitimate representation.

source.title: Named-party joinder and representative class actions

reviewedGroups.text: Party status is sometimes context-dependent in representative litigation. Absent class members may be bound by a judgment while receiving different treatment from named parties for other procedural requirements.

source.title: Who counts as a party for this question?

reviewedGroups.text: A class action allows named parties to litigate on behalf of an adequately defined group of absent persons when the requirements for representative litigation are satisfied. It can make small claims viable and resolve common issues together.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Certification is the court’s decision that a proposed group and its representatives satisfy the legal conditions for class treatment. It requires analysis of the applicable Rule 23 requirements, not simply acceptance of a class label.

Commonality requires a common contention capable of producing an answer central to the claims together. A shared label, protected status, or citation to the same statute does not necessarily supply that common answer.

Predominance asks whether common questions are sufficiently important and cohesive relative to individual questions for the proposed Rule 23(b)(3) treatment. It is more demanding than the presence of one shared question.

Adequate representation protects absentees by requiring representatives and counsel capable of pursuing the class’s interests without disqualifying conflicts. It is central to the legitimacy of binding people who do not appear individually.
Rule 23(b)(2) concerns a defendant’s action or refusal to act on grounds generally applicable to a class, making appropriate class-wide injunctive or corresponding declaratory relief.

Class identification concerns whether the group is defined so that membership can be determined and the action fairly administered. The readings report disagreement about adding a separate administrative-feasibility requirement.

source.title: Identifying the class and its members

reviewedGroups.text: Class notice informs absentees about the action, their rights, and the effect of participating or remaining in the class. The required method and opportunity to opt out depend on the category and procedural stage.

source.title: Notice and exclusion in class actions
Notice and exclusion in class actions

reviewedGroups.text: A settlement class seeks certification for resolving a controversy by an agreed compromise rather than through a class trial. Certification requirements and review of the settlement’s fairness remain distinct safeguards.

A limited-fund class addresses a situation where separate claims could exhaust a genuinely insufficient fund and impair other claimants’ recovery. Mandatory treatment requires strong justification because class members lack the ordinary damages-class opt-out choice.
Class litigation raises separate questions about subject-matter jurisdiction, Article III injury, personal jurisdiction, and venue. The relevance of absent members differs among these inquiries.

CAFA creates special federal jurisdiction and removal rules for qualifying class and mass actions. The assigned overview describes an aggregate amount requirement, specified diversity, size conditions, and exceptions.
Absent plaintiff class members do not face the same burdens as defendants compelled to defend, and the assigned cases protect them through the structure of representation and procedural safeguards.
A properly conducted class judgment can bind absentees, but its preclusive scope depends on the claims and issues actually resolved and on legitimate representation.
Issue preclusion prevents relitigation of a qualifying issue actually litigated and necessarily determined in an earlier action. It differs from a broader bar on relitigating the same claim.

source.title: Issue preclusion within the assigned materials

reviewedGroups.text: A class waiver restricts the use of representative or aggregate proceedings, often through an agreement requiring individual arbitration. Its effect can depend on federal arbitration law and the applicable contract defenses.
Preemption occurs when controlling federal law displaces a conflicting state rule. The course encounters it in arbitration, jurisdictional characterization, and enforcement of federal rights.

source.title: Federal preemption in the assigned procedural settings

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Summary judgment decides a claim or defense without trial when there is no genuine dispute of material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. It examines an evidentiary record rather than only a complaint.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: The production burden requires enough evidence to permit a reasonable factfinder to decide an issue for the party who must prove it. At summary judgment, the movant also has an initial procedural responsibility to support the motion.

The persuasion burden determines how convincingly a party must establish its claim or defense to the factfinder. The assigned discussion distinguishes preponderance, clear and convincing evidence, and proof beyond a reasonable doubt.

An inference is a conclusion drawn from evidence about an unobserved or disputed fact. At summary judgment, reasonable favorable inferences belong to the nonmovant, while credibility and weight generally remain for trial.

The judge determines governing law and whether the evidence meets legal sufficiency requirements; the jury generally decides genuinely disputed facts, credibility, and the weight of evidence in a jury case. The allocation can also become a federal-state question.

source.title: The respective roles of judge and jury

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: The assigned history traces movement from narrow collection procedures and cautious use toward the broader role associated with the 1986 trilogy. Competing concerns involve unnecessary trials, jury protection, cost, and access to proof.
A limitations period restricts the time for bringing or enforcing a claim. Its procedural treatment can affect jurisdictional strategy, the Erie inquiry, amendment, and the availability of relief.

target.title: How a civil suit can proceed

reviewedGroups.text: Forum shopping is choosing a court in light of advantages that the forum’s rules, governing law, or procedures may offer. It becomes legally significant when a doctrine seeks to prevent particular incentives or unfair differences.

target.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie

reviewedGroups.text: Statutory interpretation determines the reach of the enacted words that authorize and limit judicial action. The assigned cases use text, structure, history, and institutional consequences while disagreeing about their weight.

proposals.old: General jurisdiction extends to claims without the specific-jurisdiction link; its at-home requirement must separately be met.
